beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW + walker bookend 1: Claude composer, prompt begins 'Please use Walker to convert my game design document about …', describing this game. Eyebrow discloses it is reconstructed.
beats.narration_text: Namaste. This is Liam, in for Bear. This is Blackridge: No Way Back, a Godot game where you drive a freight van through a rainy town at night. The prompt on screen is a reconstruction; the real work began from the author's brief. Let's take apart the four particle effects this build added, and how each was tested and priced.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Blackridge: No Way Back, a narrative crime game where you drive freight through a rainy industrial town at night, into four GPU particle effects: the wiper's flick, the roof's spill on a hard brake, rain in every lamp's light, and the exhaust's vapour.
output: Every price measured; one over budget.

beats.role_note: Identifies the game, both effects, their jobs and the events and conditions that drive them.
beats.narration_text: The author chose four effects and wrote their brief. Effect A: two one-shot events, the wiper's flick at each top turn and the roof's spill on a hard brake. Effect B: two continuous ones, rain in each lamp's light and exhaust that follows the throttle. All are G P U particles in Godot four point seven point two.

It predicted ten ways they could fail, every price, and a budget of one point four five milliseconds of G P U time for all four. It was committed before the build, and Claude's project file imports it.

beats.role_note: The three parts of a particle system, a line from the scene file for each.
beats.narration_text: Every particle system has three parts, and this scene file holds all three. Emission: how many, and for how long, three hundred puffs living one point six seconds. Process: how they move and change, here its own material. Draw: what each puff looks like, a quad and its shader. The settings live in the scene, not in code.

beats.role_note: Why a GPU effect's headless price is near zero, with the recorded control.

beats.narration_text: A one's event is the van's wiper swept signal, sent every half stroke. The handler acts only at the top turn, with the wipers on. beats.role_note: Effect B1's feature that Effect A does not use: the splash sub-emitter.
beats.narration_text: B one's own feature is the sub-emitter. Drops collide with a height field, and each landing sets off a splash of three droplets. Claude's first build used hide-on-contact collisions, which in four point seven point two never set off the splash. Rigid collisions do. Neither A effect uses a sub-emitter.

beats.role_note: Effect B2's feedback code and its feature Effect A does not use.
beats.narration_text: B two's own feature is a value-driven amount ratio. After ignition it waits, ramps up from zero, then follows the throttle: point one five at idle, plus point six five times the throttle. The amount stays three hundred; only the share that emits changes. With the engine off, it's zero at once.

props.title: B2: the throttle drives amount_ratio
props.source: features/vehicles/freight_van/van_particles.gd:372–385 · Claude Code, directed by the author · verbatim
props.code:
func _drive_exhaust(delta: float) -> void:
	if not vehicle.engine_on or not exhaust.is_visible_in_tree():
		exhaust.emitting = false
		exhaust.amount_ratio = 0.0
		_ramp = 0.0
		_engine_time = IGNITION_DELAY if vehicle.engine_on else 0.0
		return
	_engine_time += delta
	if _engine_time < IGNITION_DELAY:
		return
	_ramp = move_toward(_ramp, 1.0, delta / IGNITION_RAMP)
	_throttle = move_toward(_throttle, clampf(vehicle.throttle, 0.0, 1.0), delta / THROTTLE_FOLLOW)
	exhaust.amount_ratio = (IDLE_RATIO + THROTTLE_RATIO * _throttle) * _ramp
	exhaust.emitting = true

beats.role_note: Result of B16: Effect B2 through the reverse camera, and the state test's readings of its ratio.
beats.narration_text: Through the reverse camera, less of it shows: nothing at idle or on the throttle, a narrow red column once the brake lamps light it, and a faint grey wisp after switch-off, gone a second later. The state test reads the ratio itself: point one five at idle, point eight at full throttle, zero when off, frozen while paused. In play, the dash shows that same camera.

beats.role_note: Effect B: the first strip, the tuning revision and the author's verdict.
beats.narration_text: The first B strips showed no rain, and almost no vapour. At the author's request the tuning used real drop sizes and speeds, drew each drop as the streak a camera sees, and made the exhaust a jet that stops. Around them, the lamps, the wet road and the roadside were rebuilt too, also at the author's requests. B two matched every predicted frame, B one all but two details. The author kept both.

beats.role_note: What the tests proved, the mutations that failed them, and what no headless run can show.
beats.narration_text: What the tests proved. Configuration tests read every setting back from the scenes: four hundred fifty-one checks for A one alone. State tests drive the real game through events, retriggers and pause. Both mutations, a Godot three name and a drifted spread, fail as they should, and the twenty-two earlier test runs still pass. None of this shows what the screen shows.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Please use Walker to help me tune one particle setting in my game. I will pick the setting myself. Before you change anything, ask for my prediction of what the next frame strip will show and what it will cost on the G P U, then capture the strip, measure the price, and show me predicted versus measured. It makes you commit before you look, and makes Claude measure instead of guess. Judge the answer on three things: it asks for your prediction first, shows the strip and the price, and flags any mismatch. Liam, in for Bear.
